What Babies Can Teach Us About Well-Being

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • My wife and I had a baby earlier this year, and it has revolutionized my well-being.
  • Sources indicate that when babies are born, they can only see about 20-30 cm away, and their vision is restricted to black and white.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 25, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

My wife and I had a baby earlier this year, and it has revolutionized my well-being. She is a blessing, and I want to share with you five lessons she’s taught me.

Sources indicate that when babies are born, they can only see about 20-30 cm away, and their vision is restricted to black and white. Basically, they can recognize a high-contrast boob, and that’s about it. They need to trust the people around them to take care of them, and they let you do it. Newborns don’t need training or trust funds; they just need to be confident that they’re loved and cared for.

Life flourishes when we offer love generously. We don’t expect customer service, or even reciprocity. We just want to see something thrive. This sentiment, when extended more widely, creates what I call a karmic culture. We help people because we want to live in the sort of world where people are cared for. When we need care, somebody else will be there to offer it to us. This creates a sense of safety, which promotes our thriving as much as it does a baby’s.

Recent findings suggest that my daughter likes to start the day by letting one rip. After a long nap compressed in the sling, she will similarly greet consciousness by passing gas. Ah, sweet relief. My wife and I joke that she’s a very sincere person.

There’s a lesson here. Babies don’t care what other people think of them. They certainly don’t care what’s cool or rude; they’re just following their intrinsic motivations. Now I’m not suggesting that you should be an inconsiderate bore—offending people will undermine your relationships and thus, your well-being. But it is helpful to be in touch with what you authentically want to do with your life.

In a recent development, in the early, midsummer days of sleep deprivation, I would relieve my wife of the night shift around 6 a.m. and take baby out in the stroller. Mum needed sleep but would be set off by every noise in the house, so to the park we went, and it became a habit.

As my daughter’s vision developed, I noticed her staring dumbfounded at the trees overhead. She was lost in the moment. She recently spent a good five minutes watching the autumn-coloured leaves on a bush rustle in the wind.

Sources indicate that I’d done something similar in the spring, watching a tree shimmer in the golden hour. But I had to make a conscious effort to stop, be wonderstruck, and stay mindful of the experience. I was reacting to scientific literature on the power of awe for well-being and trying to find the experience in the often-underwhelming urban environment in which I live. My daughter just did it automatically. Baby is wired for well-being. Be like baby.

Babies know the importance of rest and recovery. After a good meal and some color flash cards for brain development or a gym session ripping apart tissues, baby isn’t blue-lighting herself or otherwise hitting the dopamine button. She’s finding a dark corner in momma’s bosom and taking a nap.

In a recent development, our sleep hygiene is under threat from screens, bad diets, excessive substance use, and life stresses. People are turning to sleep tracking apps, but the irony is that you’re just contaminating your sleep space with your phone. We’re taught to give babies a dark, quiet room with a cool temperature and zero stimulus. You can do the same for yourself. Sweet dreams.

Sources indicate that when a friend’s older baby visited us last year, I studied with curiosity how much she enjoyed playing with the things in her mum’s handbag. She spent a good 15 minutes with a packet of wet wipes. Turning it over in her hands, tasting it, following Arnold Schwarzenegger’s advice to lift “down…up…” with “more energy!” She particularly enjoyed crinkling the packaging and listening to the crunchy sound it made.

Babies have a high degree of mindfulness and focus. Their baseline level of stimulus isn’t the slot machine Instagram feed or a 300-frames-per-second, cutting-edge video game. They can find joy in the everyday.

Recent findings suggest that you can too. Indeed, it’s a great way to practice savoring, a well-established technique for increasing the frequency and extending the duration of good moods. Notice things that you enjoy regularly but don’t pay attention to, like your morning coffee, favorite sweater, or how pretty your houseplants are. Take a little longer to appreciate them. Really luxuriate in the sensations and emotions they evoke in you.

Meaning and purpose in life can be enhanced by the sense that you are contributing to something bigger than yourself, and few things bring that sense home quite as powerfully as raising another human.

A key theme of terror management theory is that humans are afraid of death. We create elaborate cultural practices either to convince ourselves of immortality, as the Pharaohs did, or to feel connected to something that will persist after our death, like a nation for which we die in battle. In my experience, your baby connects you to eternity; there is a strong sense that this being carries a part of you into the future.

I am reminded of the poetry of Kalil Gibran, On Children:.

Industry observers note that and a woman who held a babe against her bosom said, Speak to us of Children. And he said: Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life’s longing for itself.

According to recent reports, you may give them your love but not your thoughts, For they have their own thoughts. You may house their bodies but not their souls, For their souls dwell in the house of tomorrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smith & Diction rebuilt the PHS brand identity around a Bloom logo, with three plants growing from the letters and Philadelphia grid underneath.

The old mark was a tree in a circle, and it noted too little about an organization that does far more than plant trees. The Pennsylvania Horticultural Society tends gardens and parks across the Philadelphia region and runs the Flower Show. The upcoming mark keeps the letters PHS as the foundation and grows three plants out of them, each drawn by Summer McClure to fit a Philadelphia city block. In deep green and burgundy on cream, mint, and sky blue, with dozens of colors in the palette, the identity looks like a garden because it behaves like one: every visit highlights something new.

The wordmark is custom, built to hold the plants like roots hold a stem. The supporting type comes from the societyâs own archive: old exhibition posters that were beautiful and hardworking, no frills, just type. Caslon Doric leads, with the confidence and clean legibility of classic newspaper headlines, and ES Park backs it up, a slab serif with geometric moments and measured softness.

Industry observers note that underneath it all sits William Pennâs original city grid. The studio baked the grid into the logo itself, then extended it through every print layout, matching the grid to the width of the flowers. Like beds in a garden, the structure keeps everything in place while each layout keeps its own personality. The mark never sits still: Henrique Barone hand-drew every frame of the plants growing, and Justin Lawes made a version that sways with the breeze.

This is a brand made to be held, not just seen. The studio printed a 42-page brand book, made a matte gold lapel pin of the mark, and built a flip book that shows the logo growing frame by frame. They matched paper tones to nearly every brand color, so the team can print in-house and stay on brand. The book cover carries the Bloom logo in dark green on mint, with an orange seal.

Recent findings suggest that the floral illustrations do more than decorate. Each one stands for a part of the organization: a flower in a cocktail glass for the Pop Up Gardens, a leafy radish for the community gardens, an oak leaf for the Healthy Neighborhoods program, a branching tree for the McLean Library. The library also gives the 2027 Philadelphia Flower Show its own peony mark, while Bre Furlongâs photographs of 18 flowers, including the tulip the studio calls the Ballerina, carry the ICONIC theme in Herbus type.

Industry observers note that located in the heart of the Mexican city of Hermosillo, Sonora, you will find Champ, a small boutique hotel. The street on which it is located is Campodónico, the surname of recognized waltz composer Rodolfo Campodónico, born in Hermosillo in 1866. He garnered a lot of recognition for his work during the early 20th century and his nickname was “Champ,” and that is from where the hotel took its name.

Industry observers note that champ celebrates the desert, the city, the local spirit and Sonoran traditions. Using imagery from old postcards and photos found in basements and thrift shops, its aim is to be as cozy and comfortable as possible for its guests.

The muted color palette was inspired by the arid northern Mexican region, where the vastness of the land and the sky reign supreme. A retro typography was chosen, since the old house where Champ is located was built in the 1970s.

Typefaces used: Pitch by Klim Type Foundry Galey by Prestigetype Studio Saa Series by URW Type Foundry Helvetica by Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann Century 725 by Heinrich Wilhelm Hoffmeister.

  • Sources indicate that what links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

Sources indicate that what links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

It has been revealed that rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents upcoming and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

It has been revealed that the show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a fresh score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

In a recent development, it accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

It has been revealed that elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

According to recent reports, for Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas states. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”.

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027.

Helsinki studio Werklig designed the identity and site for the Finnish energy company, which develops grid-balancing, baseload, and hybrid power assets across the Nordics. Featured on Fonts In Use, the web design runs on two siblings from Skriftkompani: Store Norske Skandia and Store Norske Skandia Mono. Scroll past that frosty hero and photography drops away, leaving three oversized charcoal paragraphs under a tiny About us tag to explain why Nordic grids need weather-independent power in dark winters.

Store Norske Skandia carries headlines and statements, while Store Norske Skandia Mono handles navigation, eyebrows, and captions with the crisp cadence of an engineering log. That split sharpens in the three-column What we do grid below. Three desaturated vertical photographs sit side by side: ribbed ceramic substation insulators against grey sky, a lattice transmission tower half-swallowed by mist, and an overhead power-line switch silhouetted against stark white. Beneath every frame sits an identical three-step stack â a mono tag for Balancing, Baseload, or Hybrid, a proportional subhead, and a tight monospaced caption. No rounded cards or drop shadows get in the way, so the web design reads cleanly on a single scan.

Near the bottom, winter returns up close. A wind-carved snowdrift curves across the contact band in blue-grey shadow, holding white display copy above a full-width hairline rule and [email protected]. Directly underneath, a pale-grey footer splits into four monospaced columns for Voltcore Oyâs phone line, Helsinki street address, Business ID 3638975-9, and a Back to top arrow. Itâs plain operational typography, right down to the registry number. Then the bottom strip snaps to pure white, stretching a monumental black VOLTCORE wordmark edge to edge. That final scale jump flips the compact header mark into a stark closing band for the web design.

Auto racing’s seen an explosion of flimsy “fashion wheel” brands that pretend to be high-performance. Apex is different — engineering elite racing wheels at an unmatched price point. But when we met them, customers were completely unaware of the difference. Working closely with their CEO, Eddy Pintacsi, we developed a newly introduced category vision and brand, positioning them as the category leader they are, and injecting some much-needed truth into the wheel industry.

Recent findings suggest that we started by naming the problem that Apex solves, calling it The Great Knowledge Void. A state of play where any wheel brand can make performance claims — true or not — just to make a buck. And the worst part? Customers have no way to know the difference. We went on to tell a story of how Apex is fixing this problem with their core ethos: “Real performance.” A pledge to show customers the truth — or die trying. End of story.

The identity is loud and urgent. To stop people from buying bogus wheels. The arching curves and high-contrast colors catch the eyes on the track — where it matters. And we worked with Apex to weave the same sense of urgency into how they talk about their testing standards. So that the entire industry would get with the program.

Altogether, the rebrand, POV, and messaging proves that Apex stands alone in its category. We call this a “Category of One” brand. Because when you risk everything on the track, there’s only one thing you can trust — Real Performance.

It has been revealed that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

"Is Social Security taxable?" is one of the most common tax questions retirees ask — and the answer frustrates almost everyone: it depends. Depending on your total income, anywhere from 0% to 85% of your Social Security benefits can be subject to federal income tax. The tax was introduced in 1983, originally affecting about 10% of recipients. Today, because the income thresholds were never indexed for inflation, roughly 56% of Social Security recipients pay tax on their benefits.

The good news: even in the worst case, you'll never pay tax on 100% of your Social Security. The bad news: the formula for calculating the taxable amount is one of the most convoluted in the entire tax code. In this guide, we'll break it down into plain English, show you exactly how to calculate what you owe, and — most importantly — share strategies the FI community uses to reduce or eliminate the tax entirely.

Recent findings suggest that the IRS uses a special formula called "combined income" (also called "provisional income") to determine how much of your Social Security benefits are taxable. Here's the formula:.

Combined Income = Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) + Nontaxable Interest + Half of Social Security Benefits.

The resulting number determines which taxation tier you fall into. Notice that the thresholds haven't changed since 1993 — they are not adjusted for inflation, which means more retirees cross into taxable territory every year.

Notable: "Up to 85% taxed" does not mean you pay an 85% tax rate. It means 85% of your benefits are added to your taxable income and taxed at your ordinary income rate. If you're in the 22% bracket and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you'd owe 22% on $25,500 — roughly $5,610.

This is the most common Social Security tax confusion. When the IRS indicates "up to 85% of benefits are taxable," it means 85% of your benefit amount gets added to your taxable income and taxed at your regular rate. If your marginal rate is 22% and 85% of your $30,000 benefit is taxable, you owe about $5,610 — not $25,500. The effective tax rate on your full benefit in this example is about 18.7%.

Let's walk through a real example. Meet Sarah: she's 67, single, retired, and receives $24,000 per year in Social Security benefits. She also has $18,000 in IRA withdrawals and $2,000 in municipal bond interest.

Step 1: Calculate Combined Income.

Industry observers note that step 2: Determine the Tier Sarah is single with combined income of $32,000, which falls between $25,000 and $34,000. She's in the 50% tier — up to 50% of her benefits may be taxable.

Industry observers note that step 3: Calculate the Taxable Amount The actual calculation involves comparing two formulas and taking the lesser amount. For the 50% tier:.

Sources indicate that sarah adds $3,500 to her other taxable income. At a 12% marginal rate, that's roughly $420 in additional federal tax on her Social Security.

Recent findings suggest that beyond federal taxes, 13 states also tax Social Security benefits to some degree as of 2026. Each state has its own thresholds and exemption amounts:.

Industry observers note that the remaining 37 states and Washington, D.C. do not tax Social Security benefits at all. If you're planning where to retire, this is a meaningful factor — especially if you have substantial SS benefits combined with other retirement income.

Once you reach age 70.5, you can donate up to $105,000 per year directly from your IRA to a qualified charity. A step-by-step walkthrough for estimating what you owe.

List your AGI from all sources: IRA/401(k) withdrawals, pension income, wages, dividends, capital gains, rental income. Get your total Social Security benefit from your SSA-1099 form.

Pro tip: Don't forget nontaxable municipal bond interest — it counts in the combined income formula even though it's not on your 1040.

Add your AGI + nontaxable interest + half of your Social Security benefits. This "combined income" number determines your taxation tier.

According to recent reports, compare your combined income to the thresholds: Single — $25K (50% tier), $34K (85% tier). Married filing jointly — $32K (50% tier), $44K (85% tier).

Sources indicate that for the 50% tier: take 50% of combined income above the lower threshold (capped at 50% of benefits). For the 85% tier: the calculation is more complex — use IRS Publication 915 worksheet or tax software.

Industry observers note that pro tip: Tax software handles this automatically. If doing it by hand, IRS Publication 915 has the complete worksheet.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Dinner Ladies needed a recipe for a rebrand that would not only pay respect to their unique origin story but bring their visual and verbal identity up to speed with their growth as Australia’s tastiest frozen meal service. We joined forces to cook them up a fresh look and feel that reflects their homely meals and anti-“mumsy” attitude, extending all the way from their website through to their packaging. Now whack the oven on, because Australia’s hottest frozen meal service has arrived.

Since it all began with two determined women in a Sydney-side backyard shed in 2007, The Dinner Ladies have been filling the freezers, bellies and hearts of thousands of busy Australian families with their ready-to-heat comfort meals. Born from a deep understanding of dinner time chaos, and the desire to bring some ease back into this routine, The Dinner Ladies’ commitment to delivering meals worthy of mum’s tick of approval remains unwavering.

The market for pre-prepared meal delivery is an oversaturated landscape steeped in clichés and same-same messaging that claims to be the most healthy, convenient or delicious dinnertime solution. They not only lack a distinct personality but also relatability to their customer — time-poor people who just want simple, genuinely good, homemade meals that help take the pressure off when it’s needed most. This is where The Dinner Ladies shine. A flavour-stacked service that takes care of dinner, so you can focus on doing life.

The brand had become known and loved for their unexpected, no nonsense and slightly audacious approach. This was not only refreshingly real but a reflection of both their wholesome offering and the founding ladies. However, over seventeen years of brand iterations their look had become diluted, lost its attitudinal punch, and needed a massive serve of reinvigoration. Our vision was to bring back the best from their history and turn up the heat across the board to let the nation know they mean (meal delivery) business.

We fully immersed ourselves in The Dinner Ladies story, from taking a deep dive through past website designs and hand drawn logos on a napkin, to visiting the shed where it all began and the factory where it now thrives. This helped us draw out the strongest existing brand elements, like their early trad-tattoo-esque illustrations and counter-“mumsy” stereotype, and turn them into a modern evolution. Driven by “Food from the Heart,” each component of the visual identity communicates the brand essence and no-BS confidence of a service that truly helps take the stress out of dinnertime.

In a recent development, the first step was the refinement of the logo. By decoupling the heart and the script, we gave it flexibility, made it easier to read at every touchpoint and allowed it to scale as needed. The custom heart logo was designed by us and then, alongside the wordmark, handed to illustrator Jake Foreman to redraw and personalise with his iconic texture and gritty stipple.

In a recent development, the Dinner Ladies’ existing red already had distinct brand attribution in the category so we just refined it with a bright and modern twist. The secondary palette supports our hero red with a balance of warm, approachable and slightly retro hues. When united, the system unlocks a number of interesting and vibrant combinations that are particularly useful across hard-working digital applications.

We used the typeface Denim by Displaay Type Foundry to show off the brand’s confident personality yet retain practicality. Denim Wide’s used in headings and call-to-action applications to command attention, while its regular cut counterpart rounds out the system with a friendly, clean and legible option for subheadings and body copy. With its subtle details, the typeface can be an attention-grabbing hero element that showcases the bold tone of voice but also work alongside more expressive moments.

Sources indicate that the tone of voice needed to capture the brand’s joyful, cheeky yet comforting personality, while steering clear of any patronising “mumsy” tropes and stereotypes. We worked with copywriter Cat Wall to develop a verbal identity that balanced the empathetic caregiver with the charmingly rebellious tone of the ladies themselves. In a category saturated with over-sincerity and fake friendliness, the tone offers a refreshing sprinkle of irreverence with a straight-forward, bull-free reflection of the audience and their needs.

Sources indicate that the photography celebrates the authentic messiness of real life dinnertime. A reflection of the brand’s tell-it-like-it-is attitude, the shoot didn’t shy away from capturing raw moments — the remnants of a great dish alongside a newly introduced one being served or a bolognese-faced baby — mixed with the joy of sharing generous, mouth-watering food.

With Alana Dimou behind the lens, Jerrie-Joy Redman-Lloyd on styling, Oriana De Luca on wardrobe, Gavin Anesbury with a hair and makeup brush in hand, and Michaela Le on production, the brand came to life. Warm, natural lighting, combined with quirky styling choices, pops of colour or pattern and intentional (and encouraged) chaos set a homely and inviting scene with a pinch of rebellion.

Illustration has always been a major piece of The Dinner Ladies’ brand so we wanted to bring it across to the rebrand. The original illustrations’ punk and rough-around-the-edges flair drew us to references of traditional trad tattoos.

It has been revealed that collaborating further with illustrator Jake Foreman, we crafted a suite of illustrations that served as both personality-rich storytelling pieces and functional devices. While the small scenes and spots speak to specific offerings of the brand, the hero illustration speaks to the love behind every Dinner Ladies dish and the comforting shared experiences created around the table.

These illustrations are supported by our suite of type-furniture elements that not only support the main design elements but add character to any layout.

As a product that’s often shoved into the freezer and then reached for in a rush, legibility and easy differentiation were priorities for designing the packaging. A simple colour-coded system helps to distinguish between protein groups at a glance, making it quick and effortless to find the crowd-pleasing meal that’s ready to save the day.

In a recent development, the Dinner Ladies now have a brand that not only celebrates their seventeen year legacy but gives them the tools for future decades of success. The flexible design system and punchy tone of voice pays tribute to their tenacious past, the founding ladies behind the service and their wholesome mission put joy back into dinner time. Now The Dinner Ladies can stand loud and proud with a brand that reflects their readiness to dish up delicious dinners to an entire nation.

  • Sotheby’s today unveiled that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890).
  • The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”.
  • The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sotheby’s today unveiled that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in Upcoming York.

The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

Industry observers note that the Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”.

The provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

According to recent reports, last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he claims took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”.

The Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a latest generation of collectors.”.

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

Latest Update: Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century.
  • The repatriation is part of a university initiative introduced in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands.
  • Sources indicate that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative introduced in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

Sources indicate that the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

Industry observers note that the Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil.

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, remarked during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

Sources indicate that brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she noted. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

Recent findings suggest that A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

In a recent development, more than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown.
  • Sources indicate that traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an Australian first, WHEN provides at-home egg count testing and access to the country’s leading fertility experts — prompting a conversation about how and when people can access their own fertility information. They came to us to conceive a brand that could balance credibility and compassion in equal measure. One that felt just as comfortable in a trusted doctor’s office as the shiny shelves of a global beauty store.

The conversation about fertility for people with ovaries has traditionally centred around the biological clock’s looming countdown. But with all that focus on the fear-inducing countdown, there’s not a lot of helpful talk — about how fertility works, the proactive steps we can take to improve it, or why the biological clock is an outdated trope. That’s where WHEN comes in — a fertility medtech organization on a mission to ensure no one with ovaries is left wondering about them.

Sources indicate that traditionally, brands in the fertility space are designed to build trust in their medical expertise. But this narrow focus has resulted in a category that feels overly clinical and sometimes cold, losing sight of the real people at the heart of it all. We saw an opportunity to create something that balanced the two — trust and credibility, with warmth and humanity. A direct-to-consumer lifestyle brand built on deep medical experience that felt equally at home in a retail environment.

In a recent development, fertility is, understandably, incredibly personal and seldom discussed. To get to the heart of the matter, our friends at VML conducted a series of focus groups, one-on-one interviews and stakeholder research. Because in failing to talk about it, we’re failing to give people the information they need at the right time. People are proactive about pap smears, mammograms, skin checks, sexual health tests—all considered lead indicators that look ahead to impact the future. But fertility is measured as a lag indicator, only measured once it’s more difficult to affect the outcome.

Industry observers note that without jumping through costly medical hoops, there is no accessible way for people to know what’s happening inside their very own bodies without a referral. The medical industry is not set up to provide this kind of information proactively, which can make people feel blocked. And when it comes to fertility, information is power.

Sources indicate that given WHEN is the first of its kind in Australia, care needed to be taken to communicate the importance and impact of its service. Credible medical expertise was a leading reason to believe. But we also knew people needed to hear the real stories behind the brand to build trust in something so upcoming. Striking the balance was critical.

The result is a visual and verbal system that blends emotion with science, expression with information. Designed to showcase fertility stories, expert advice and the endless questions we ask ourselves, the brand moves seamlessly from packaging to print, retail stores to social media.

Sources indicate that the WHEN wordmark sits at the heart of the visual identity. Clear and confident, it anchors the brand as a dependable figure in the health and medical space. Paired with an organic cell shape that reacts to the world around it, the wordmark and logoform are a perfect foil to the other. Together, they represent standing strong amid the ever-changing nature of life.

WHEN’s typeface is ABC Diatype. It’s used for everything — from wordmark to body copy. Chosen for its modernity and scientific edge, it brings calm and clarity to everything we say. Paired with a colour palette of lemon and neutrals, the identity feels light and warm against an industry so often cold and clinical.

According to recent reports, an important first touchpoint was the at-home testing kit — the Egg Count Check. The kit is split into three sections: Prepare, Collect, and Send. We designed the packaging experience to follow the same logical structure, ensuring the steps were simple to follow and easy to use.

It has been revealed that inspired by the sleek aesthetic of our favourite tech brands, the kit’s box takes a rigid form with special attention paid to premium print finishes. We also created a custom instruction booklet to guide the user through the process, designed and illustrated in-house.

Our primary photography style uses intimate portraits and close crops to focus on the subject’s internal thoughts and feelings. We aim to capture moments that feel like a natural extension of everyday life, empowering and relatable in their familiarity. As a secondary style, we splice natural textures and fluid forms with our portraits, like fragments of memory telling the story of a person’s inner world.

It has been revealed that to further enhance this sense of intimacy, a series of icons were developed to capture the different states of mind one might feel around this sensitive and personal topic. Following the same visual language as the logo, these icons add flexibility and expression to the brand, especially when used with the intimate portraiture.

According to recent reports, the brand name itself is a question — when? But it’s also a statement of intent. We worked with copywriter Amy Scott to develop a verbal concept exploring the idea of an inner monologue, giving voice to the questions we ask ourselves but perhaps never verbalise. The brand speaks as an empathetic expert, both insightful and inclusive. By creating space for open conversation and asking the questions people ask themselves, we show no matter where they’re at in their fertility journey, they’re not alone.

WHEN doesn’t only set to change fertility testing, but to also facilitate an aspirational platform that aims to drive community and empowering conversation around fertility. The brand was crafted to grow into a multidimensional platform for fertility information access and support. We helped design the first step of this journey through WHEN Matters — a curated blog for sharing real fertility stories and credible medical expertise to ensure no one with ovaries was left feeling alone on their journey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

The mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

According to recent reports, the type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

In a recent development, spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

Recent findings suggest that the identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron states the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Industry observers note that saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert upcoming audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz notes the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

See the full Zero 10 case study from Saffron.

Drawing from historical horticultural publications, plant glossaries and garden almanacs, 1/1 Studio developed a design language that honours the depth of knowledge and integrity inherent in Field Studies Flora’s practice. The site functions as both a gallery of case studies and an educational resource, inviting visitors into a world where botanical understanding and artistic expression converge.

According to recent reports, the visual identity and website design emphasise documentation and craft, mirroring the studio’s meticulous approach to their work. The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

According to recent reports, feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

In a recent development, the FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

It has been revealed that how you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

In a recent development, two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

Recent findings suggest that the resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a fresh opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

Sources indicate that what not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice notes never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to manufacturer changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

In a recent development, health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:.

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

Sources indicate that ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

Industry observers note that A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Sources indicate that have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the problem your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

It has been revealed that verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

It has been revealed that before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the matter 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

It has been revealed that pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream tech giant in three years.

In a recent development, at minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

According to recent reports, be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees).
  • Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, noted in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades.
  • Sources indicate that sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A striking limestone head by Amedeo Modigliani sold for $44.6m (with fees) at Phillips Modern and contemporary evening sale last night (17 November), leading a nearly sold-out auction totalling $85.75m ($104.4m with fees). That is an increase of 55% from the same sale last November, which topped out at $54.8m ($67.3m with fees).

Robert Manley, Phillips’ chairman and worldwide head of Modern and contemporary art, noted in a statement that there had been strong bidding across Modern, post-war and contemporary art: “Nearly 90% of the works offered had never been previously sold at auction, with many of the sale’s works coming from esteemed private collections where they had been for decades. Tonight’s results are a powerful reminder that truly exceptional works continue to inspire extraordinary competition in the market.”.

Sources indicate that sales were brisk in a bustling room, the pace in part due to the large number of works backed by third party guarantees. With just 22 lots on offer—the house withdrew Derek Fordjour’s Haberdasher, estimated at $350,000 to $550,000, at the last minute—14 carried a guarantee.

It took less than a minute and a half, for instance, for auctioneer Henry Highley to hammer Claude Monet’s La Maison dans les roses (1925) at $3.2m, matching the $4m high estimate with fees.

Claude Monet's La Maison dans les roses.

On the other hand, the Modigliani, also guaranteed, sparked a ten-minute three-way battle, escalating from the starting bid of $18m to $28m in just a few seconds before slowing to $100,000 increments. A phone bidder speaking with Phillips specialist India Phillips ultimately prevailed over clients on the line with specialists Jeremiah Evarts and Kevie Yang, placing the winning bid at $38.2m ($44.6m with fees) on an estimate of $28m to $35m.

In a recent development, the piece, dating from 1911 to 1912, is one of just 28 sculptures by the artist, and part of a larger series of limestone heads each titled Tête. The price, while impressive, failed to approach the $70.7m achieved by another work from the series at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in 2014, which remains the record for Modigliani sculptures. His painting record, $170.4m for the 1918 painting Nu couché—the sixth most expensive work ever to sell at auction—dates to the following year.

According to recent reports, the evening’s second-biggest lot was David Hockney’s eight-panel oil painting David, Celia, Stephen and Ian, London 1982, which sold for $10m ($12.2m with fees) within its $10m to $15m estimate. The artist, who died in June at the age of 88, made the work in 1982. It reflects his experiments at the time with photographing a subject from slightly different, overlapping viewpoints to create Cubist-inspired collages, and marks Hockney’s return to painting after a period focused on photography.

Helen Frankenthaler's Seabreeze.

The painting, which was sold by the Joel and Carole Bernstein family collection, also boasts an impressive museum pedigree, including appearances at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the National Portrait Gallery in London.

Rounding out the sale’s top three was Alexander Calder’s 1959 mobile Snow Flurry, May 14—one of the few works without a third-party guarantee, and being sold by the family of Brazilian art critic Mário Pedrosa. Yang caused some excitement when she raised her bid straight from $4.6m to $6m, a price no one else was willing to top. The total with fees was $7.5m, above a high estimate of $6m.

Helen Frankenthaler had the sale’s top result for a woman artist with Seabreeze (1980), which went for $4.5m (with fees). Frankenthaler followed that up a few lots later with Peacock Alley (1990) $2.7m (with fees), right in the middle of its $2m to $3m estimate.

Industry observers note that the night’s only bought-in lot was Anselm Kiefer’s Melancholia (2005), which carried an estimate of $650,000 to $850,000, but bidding stalled out at just $500,000. The rust-coated painting features a polyhedral glass-and-iron sculpture mounted on the canvas.

David Hockney's David, Celia, Stephen, Ian, London August 1982 (Four Friends) (1982).

And while Jackson Pollock’s 1946 abstraction Constellation did find a buyer, the work failed to meet its low estimate of $3.5m. Despite the current show of Pollock and his wife Lee Krasner uptown at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and a provenance boasting the legendary dealer Peggy Guggenheim, the work hammered at just $2.6m ($3.3m with fees). Frank Stella’s Port Tampa City, from the estate of the late dealer Robert Mnuchin, also hammered below estimate, at $2.8m ($3.5m with fees) despite an estimate of $3m to $5m. The orange canvas, in the shape of an eight-point star quilt block, dates to 1963.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, both paintings made the sale’s top ten list, slotting in at number eight for Stella and nine for Pollock, just above the second Frankenthaler. Other noteworthy results included Clyfford Still’s PH-589 (1959). Expected to sell for $4m to $6m, it hammered for $4.2m ($5.3m with fees) to an online bidder from Tel Aviv.

It doesnât rely on bloated toolbars or floating menus â every click turns the web design into a compact audiovisual synthesizer.

Clicking the bottom arrow flips the palette straight to black with red registration dots, introducing Petrilloâs studio overview and his bottega positioning alongside a vertical red HELLO! tab and a yellow Tamber audio card peeking up from below. Tapping WORK opens a single-column stack of charcoal project cards pairing crisp square emblems with discipline tags for The Clock Experience, Tamber, Deeds, Wise Data Vis, and Vast Bank. Deeper down the studio page, three oversized red-and-black geometric squircle modules divide the practice into BRAND, PRODUCT, and MARKETING above plain email and journal links. Kandinsky record and trove consigned by Jeff Koons buoy Christie’s 20th-century sale in New York

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Upcoming York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.
  • Recent findings suggest that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees).
  • According to recent reports, thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buoyed by a handful of gems, Christie’s 20th-century evening sale on 17 November in Upcoming York racked up $521m, or $627m with fees, underscoring the allure of rare-to-market trophy works.

Recent findings suggest that the hammer total hit the low-side of the $511m-$743m pre-sale estimate (all estimates calculated without fees). The result was a marked improvement on last November’s equivalent sale, which made $390.1m, or $471.7m with fees.

According to recent reports, thirty one of the 75 lots offered were backed by third party guarantees and a further five by house guarantees. Three multi-million dollar offerings were withdrawn from the sale, including an Andy Warhol self portrait, estimated between $14m-$18m.

According to recent reports, it wasn’t a perfect evening: six lots failed to sell. These included a small-scale group of seven Jackson Pollock paintings from the 1950s (est $7m-$9m); a 1915 Modigliani painting Beatrice Hastings sitting (est $5m-$7m); and a 1945 Léger canvas (est $1.2m-$1.8m). Including the three withdrawn lots, this amounted to an 88% sell through rate.

Still, six artist records were set, including the 11-ft high Fernando Botero bronze, Horse (2006), which was parked on the sidewalk in front of Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, and made $4.2m ($5.2m with fees).

The marathon evening got off to a modest start with Mary Bauermeister’s wooden box construction packed with optical elements, Nature Mort (1967-69), which made $100,000 ($128,000 with fees), the first from the collection of investment banker and art scholar Herbert Lust.

The Lust trove of eight works (a Frank Stella estimated at $7m-$10m was withdrawn before the sale) realised $42m with fees, topped by Alberto Giacometti’s impossibly thin, 119cm-high bronze, Figure, demie grandeur (no.2) from 1949 that made $22m ($25.9m with fees), against an estimate of $20m-$30m.

Beyond Lust, a late and untitled Mark Rothko acrylic on paper laid down on canvas in fiery red hues from 1968 made $11.5m ($13.9m with fees) and Philip Guston’s feather light brush strokes in Painting from 1952 sold for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees), topping out the few Ab-Ex offerings.

It has been revealed that the evening featured two mega-priced lots, both estimated at $60m-$80m. Wassily Kandinsky’s Weimar-era abstraction Betonte Ecken (accentuated corners, 1923), which once owned by the Guggenheim Museum co-founder Hilla Rebay, soared to a record $74m ($85.8m with fees). The anonymous seller acquired it at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in May 1986 for $1m.

Gustav Klimt’s dazzling lakeside composition, Litzlbergkeller from 1915-16, was observed and painted by Klimt with the aid of a telescope positioned and capturing the stout likeness of the Austrian inn he frequented for eight idyllic summers. It floated to $71m ($82.3m with fees).

Alex Rotter, Christie’s global president, nabbed both works for anonymous clients on his rainmaking telephone.

The Klimt had been acquired by last night's consignor at Sotheby’s Fresh York in May 1997 from the estate of Neue Galerie co-founder Serge Sabarsky for a then-record $14.4m.

It has been revealed that A standout of the season, Wilfredo Lam’s large, tropical-inspired composition executed in a Magical Realism style, Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l’herbe des dieux) from 1943, made a record $9.5m ($11.6m with fees). It debuted at the Pierre Matisse Gallery in 1944 and was recently featured in the Museum of Modern Art retrospective Wilfredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s New York in November 1997 for $1.3m with fees. The Lam came to market backed by a third-party guarantee.

In a recent development, impressionist era paintings were also in rich supply. Paul Cézanne’s luscious tabletop still life Tasse, verre et fruits (around 1877) was consigned by the 86-year-old billionaire businessman William I. Koch. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees).

The Cézanne was once owned by the former Dutch banker Siegfried Kramarsky, whose estate sold Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr Gachet from 1890 at Christie’s Latest York in May 1990 for a then-record $82.5m with fees.

In a recent development, french painting masters continued with Camille Pissarro’s evocative and crowded Parisian cityscape (sans protesters), Le Pont-Neuf, après-midi de pluie, 1re série from 1901 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees). It last sold at Christie’s New York in November 2019 for $6.5m with fees.

Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s Hercules and Achelous (1590).

Big name consignors were not in short supply as evidenced by a trove of Picassos and several Old Master works under the marketing title “Heroes & Lovers: Property of a Distinguished Collector”—also known as Jeff Koons.

The group was led by Picasso’s snogging couple, Le Baiser (October 1969), which is famed in part for its inclusion in the artist’s late paintings exhibition in Avignon at the Palais des Papes in 1970, and went for $26.5m ($31.1m with fees).

The monochrome composition depicting the artist and his wife and muse Jacqueline Roque conveys both passion and love in the artist’s last decade. Though a relatively big price, it came nowhere near its $40-$60m estimate.

Backed by a third-party guarantee, the work was acquired by Koons from Sotheby’s New York in May 2008 for $17.4m, the same year his Balloon flower-Magenta from 1995-2000 sold at Christies London for £12.9m, or $25.7m.

Industry observers note that picasso’s Tête de femme (Dora Maar), painted in wartime Paris on 25 May 1941 sold for $25.5m ($30m with fees). Another Dora Maar split-angle composition with her face featured alongside her rival Marie-Therese Walther from 1939-40 brought $6m ($7.4m with fees) against an unrealistic estimate of $10m-$15m.

The Koons trove, backed by third party guarantees also included a trio of Old Master works, topped by Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s dramatic, mythological depiction of Hercules and Achelous from 1590, and hugely scaled at 91.45cm by 242.57cm. It brought $11.5m ($13.9m with fees), below its $12m-$18m estimate but enough to once again set the artist's record. Koons acquired it at Christie’s New York in April 2008 for a then-record $8.1 million. All in, the Koons group tallied $104.7m with fees.

Recent findings suggest that willem de Kooning’s rushing Yellow River from 1958, deaccessioned by the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York “to benefit the collection", and once described by the late critic Thomas B. Hess as “abstract parkway landscapes”, made $9m ($11m with fees).

Recent findings suggest that one of the best back stories of the season came courtesy of Georgia O’Keeffe’s Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I (1930), which was found buried in a trunk by the niece of the East Village owner who received it as a college graduation present in 1963. Rarely does one see property titles from the East Village. One newspaper article said the elderly owner, a former Foreign Service member, decided to hide the painting away in the mid 1980s after one visitor eyed it and she grew suspicious.

Industry observers note that it hasn’t been seen in public since 1931 when it was featured in Alfred Stieglitz’s An American Place gallery solo show of the artist. It made $3.9m ($4.8m with fees).

Another version of the curvy sand hills of the Rio Grande Valley composition where O’Keeffe had her studio sold at Christie’s Newly introduced York in May 2018 from the collection of Peggy and David Rockefeller for $8.4m.

Though the Frida Kahlo painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (1952) was withdrawn at the 11th hour over export issues, her husband Diego Rivera fared better, with the floral Vendedora de flores, de Tehauntepec (1929) blossoming at $8.1m ($9.9m with fees). It blew past its $3.5m high estimate—another winner for the William I. Koch collection which all in realised $66.3m.

In a recent development, “It felt like a very calibrated evening with a solid but measured pace,” said Adrien Meyer, Christie’s auctioneer, as he exited the salesroom. “There was significant participation from Asia that I haven’t seen in a while.”.

The evening action resumes Wednesday at Sotheby’s and the awaited offering of a $180m Vincent van Gogh painting Châtaigniers en fleurs from 1890.

How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design
